title: Ethiopian Somali Suqaar
community: Somali Region (Ogaden) — the Ethiopian Somali community
author: Chef Haile

heritage.origin: Somali Region of Ethiopia — the Ogaden, home to Ethiopian Somali communities
heritage.history: The Somali Region (formerly Ogaden) is the eastern lowland area of Ethiopia bordering Somalia. The Ethiopian Somali community shares food culture with Somalia while having developed distinct regional variations. Suqaar is the quick-cooked diced meat dish of Somali cuisine — cubed beef or goat quickly sautéed with onion, tomato, sweet pepper, and Somali spice blend. It is significantly milder than Amhara wat but more aromatic from the cumin and coriander that dominate the Somali spice tradition.

desc: Ethiopian Somali Suqaar — diced beef or goat quickly sautéed with onion, tomato, sweet pepper, cumin, and coriander. The fast-cooked meat dish of the eastern Ethiopian Somali community — aromatic, lightly spiced, and completely different from the berbere-based highland wats.
longDesc: Suqaar is the Somali approach to fast meat cooking — the small cubes cook in minutes, the spices are aromatic rather than hot, and the result is a dish entirely different from highland Ethiopian cooking. It is served with rice or Somali canjeero (thin flatbread).
ingredients: 500g beef or goat — cut into 1cm cubes
steps: Add meat cubes. Sear without stirring 2 minutes.
Add garlic, spices, tomatoes, and sweet pepper.
Stir and cook 5—6 minutes until everything is combined and cooked through.
chefTips: High heat and quick cooking — suqaar is not a slow stew.
commonMistakes: Adding berbere — completely changes the character.
Slow cooking — suqaar is fast food.
cookingScience: The 1cm cube size is optimal for rapid cooking — small enough to cook through in 5—6 minutes at high heat while still retaining moisture within each cube.
sustainabilityTips: Goat is common in the Somali Region — drought-resistant and sustainable in arid environments.
culturalNote: Ethiopian Somali Suqaar is the food that demonstrates how Ethiopia's eastern regions connect to the broader Horn of Africa food culture — the Somali spice tradition, the quick-cook technique, and the preference for rice over injera all speak to a cuisine shaped by the Indian Ocean trade routes.
